title: Poached Eggs
subtitle: Perfectly set white with a runny yolk
excerpt: Eggs slid gently into barely simmering water acidulated with a splash of white wine vinegar, and cooked for 3 minutes until the white is just set and the yolk is warm and runny inside.

recipe.sourceNotes: Poached eggs are one of the fundamentals of British breakfast cooking. The two keys are using very fresh eggs (the white clings tighter to the yolk) and keeping the water at a very gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil. The splash of white wine vinegar helps the white coagulate faster around the yolk. The swirling vortex method is optional; cracking the egg into a small cup first and lowering it close to the water surface is the more reliable technique.

recipeTools.notes: Wide, shallow pan for the eggs.

content.text: The water must be barely simmering: a rolling boil breaks the white apart. Crack each egg into a small cup or ramekin before sliding it into the water. This prevents shell fragments in the pan and gives you control over the drop. Fresh eggs produce a neater result than older ones.

Fill a wide, shallow saucepan with 8 cm of water. Add the white wine vinegar. Bring to a very gentle simmer over medium heat. The water should have small bubbles rising slowly from the base, not a rolling boil.

Crack each egg into a small cup. Holding the cup close to the surface of the water, tip the egg in gently. You can poach 2 to 3 eggs at a time. Cook for 3 minutes for a runny yolk, 4 minutes for a firmer set.
Lift each egg out with a slotted spoon. Drain on a folded piece of kitchen paper. Serve immediately on buttered toast. Season with salt and pepper at the table.
